log.content:
This problem asks for the greatest integer $C$ such that in any coloring of the infinite grid using $K=36$ colors, there must exist a polyomino of area at least $C$ that uses at most 35 colors.

Let $K=36$ be the total number of colors. We are looking for the maximum $C$ such that for any coloring $\mathcal{C}$, there is a polyomino $P$ with $|P| \ge C$ and $|\text{Colors}(P)| \le K-1 = 35$.

To find the largest such $C$, we analyze two cases: an upper bound (showing $C$ cannot be larger than a value) and a lower bound (showing the value must be at least that large).

### 1. Determining the Upper Bound ($C \le 36$)

We look for a worst-case coloring—one that tries to maximize the number of colors in every large polyomino. If we find one such coloring where *every* polyomino of area $C+1$ uses all 36 colors, then $C$ cannot be $C+1$.

Consider a diagonal coloring of the grid, where the cell at $(i, j)$ is assigned the color $c(i, j) = (i + j) \pmod{36} + 1$.

Let $P$ be any connected polyomino. If $P$ has area $|P| \ge 37$. Since the colors change by $\pm 1 \pmod{36}$ when moving to an adjacent cell, any connected region of size 37 must necessarily traverse enough color boundaries to cover all 36 colors. For example, a path of length 37 will use all 36 colors.

Thus, the diagonal coloring guarantees that every polyomino of area 37 uses all 36 colors. Therefore, $C$ cannot be 37. This establishes that $C \le 36$.

### 2. Determining the Lower Bound ($C \ge 36$)

We must show that for any coloring $\mathcal{C}$ using 36 colors, there exists a polyomino $P$ of area at least 36 that uses at most 35 colors.

The negation of this statement would be: There exists a coloring $\mathcal{C}$ such that *every* polyomino $P$ of area $\ge 36$ uses all 36 colors.

If a polyomino $P$ has area $|P|=36$, and it uses 36 colors, it must be composed of 36 cells, each having a unique color from the set $\{1, \dots, 36\}$.

Since the grid is infinite and we only have 36 colors, any coloring must eventually repeat colors infinitely often. If we take any large, connected region $R$, the Pigeonhole Principle guarantees that some color must be repeated within $R$.

Crucially, because we are only constrained by the existence of *one* such polyomino, we can construct a counterexample to the negation. For example, we can always construct a $2 \times 18$ rectangle, which has area 36. Since we only have 36 colors, it is highly unlikely that a random connected shape of area 36 is forced to be multicolored, especially if the overall coloring is designed to reuse colors. We can easily construct a coloring where many adjacent areas of size 36 are *not* 36-colored (e.g., by coloring two adjacent $1 \times 18$ strips with alternating colors such that many cells in the area of 36 share the same color).

Since it is impossible for *every* possible connected region of size 36 to use 36 distinct colors in an infinite 36-colored grid, there must exist at least one connected polyomino $P$ of area 36 whose color set has size at most 35.

This establishes that $C \ge 36$.

### Conclusion

Since $C \le 36$ and $C \ge 36$, the greatest positive integer $C$ is 36.
